KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
A slow-moving front is situated in the vicinity of the eastern Great 
Lakes and St Lawrence River Valley this afternoon. Aloft, a 500mb 
shortwave will intersect this front and result in the development of 
isolated to scattered showers, mainly in and around the mountains 
this afternoon and evening. Elsewhere, partly sunny conditions 
prevail with afternoon temps in the mid 70s to low 80s. 

Also keeping an eye on an area of marine fog and stratus on latest 
satellite imagery. This could bring reduced visibilities as early 
as this afternoon along the Maine coastline before potentially
spreading inland this evening and tonight, especially along and
east of the I-95 corridor from Portland to Augusta and 
Waterville, where fog could be locally dense. Aside from this 
area, patchy fog could develop in many areas tonight, especially
within and near river valleys. Overnight lows will range from 
the 50s to lower 60s.

Fog will lift by mid-morning Thursday, and another seasonable day is 
expected temperature-wise with highs in the mid 70s to lower 80s. 
The previously mentioned front will push into New England, and while 
most will stay dry, a few showers may develop during the afternoon 
and evening while clouds increase across the area. A somewhat better 
chance of showers will be across southern NH and perhaps far SW 
Maine as a more-defined wave moves across southern New England. The 
last couple runs of the HRRR have trended toward this while other 
models keep the precip more suppressed to the south. For now PoPs 
are 20-30% in this area, but may need to be raised or lowered with 
how model trends go. Either way, amounts are expected to be 
light and a tenth of an inch or less.

If the showers materialize, they should end by or shortly after 
midnight Thursday night. More valley fog possible overnight, and 
lows will be a tad cooler than tonight with most 50s, except 40s in 
some of the northern valleys. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Shortwave ridging builds in Friday behind the departing trough 
with high pressure looking to move in and dominate in our 
forecast area. For Friday, temperatures will generally hold in 
the mid to upper 70s, with a few places in Southern New 
Hampshire flirting with the 80 degree mark. Once again, as for 
most of the summer, a seabreeze should kick in during the 
afternoon, dropping temperatures near the coastline a few 
degrees come time early evening. Overnight temperatures should 
stick to the mid to upper 50s as well. Looking ahead to the 
weekend, models are mixed on when the first batch of 
precipitation moves into our area for Saturday. Here, a 500 mb 
low from our west joins up with approaching moisture from our 
south. Some deterministic models, are a bit unsure of the 
positioning of this trough and its associated moisture with 
long- range solutions like the Canadian and European bring 
precipitation into southern areas of our CWA by Saturday 
afternoon, while the GFS holds back on widespread precip 
overall. Knowing this, it would be better to see some agreement 
in the models regarding precip because, as of right now, it is 
too early to tell when this potential batch of precipitation 
moves in, but trends will be monitored in the coming days to 
figure out whether Saturday will be dry or wet. At the moment, 
PoPs are generally in the 20-40% range over our portions of our 
CWA by late in the day on Saturday. In terms of temperatures, 
highs will be in the upper 60s to low 70s. 

As stated above, rain chances could further increase Saturday 
night into Sunday as the 500mb works its way in and covers most 
of the Eastern Seaboard. A strong signal from ensembles shows 
our area seeing measurable rain with models hinting at greater 
than a quarter of an inch for most of our CWA, with the 
potential for heavier amounts of rainfall along the immediate 
coastline and at higher elevations. At the moment, this 500 mb 
trough looks to remain an open wave, but this could change if it
closes off, to which a slower onset and end of precipitation 
will likely be the result. If the trough closes off, the slower 
onset and end could come to fruition, where in this case, 
precipitation could have trouble ending by the start of next 
week. Overnight Sunday, rain could be clearing out away from the
coastline, but upslope showers could continue through early 
Monday morning. 

Drying conditions should generally dominate going into early 
next week, with long range models still hinting at chances for 
upslope showers continuing into the middle of next week. These 
upslope shower chances will wane as the week progresses, with 
some models showing near zero rain probabilities as early as 
Tuesday, along with high pressure returning to our area. On the 
temperature side starting next week, highs look to be average 
for this time of year staying in the mid to upper 70s with 
nightly lows in the mid 50s to low 60s.
